prompt: Where does the latency that `pl latency` reports come from, in this lab?

choices.text: A timer around each call to the stand-in, measured on your machine
choices.why: It is not measured: two runs print the same numbers.

choices.text: The provider's published latency table for the model
choices.why: No provider is involved; the numbers are the course's.

choices.text: Arithmetic on declared numbers
choices.why: Right: per call, per input token, per output token, plus jitter.

choices.text: The length of the prompt file in bytes, read from disk
choices.why: Bytes on disk play no part; tokens do.

prompt: Using `LATENCY` and the per-call tokens of `v3-examples` (238.5 in, 37.4 out), what is the latency of an average call before jitter, in milliseconds?
`v3-examples` sends three times the input of `v2-json`, yet its p95 is lower. Why?

choices.text: The examples are cached between calls, so after the first call the stand-in reads them for free
choices.why: Neither prompt turns the cache on.

choices.text: It writes fewer output tokens, and each costs fifty times an input token
choices.why: Right: 37.4 against 39.9 a call, and a longest answer of 46 against 50.

choices.text: Input tokens cost nothing in the stand-in
choices.why: They cost 0.4 ms each: 64 ms more for v3.

choices.text: Jitter
choices.why: Jitter is at most 150 ms and cannot explain a consistent shape.

prompt: `pl latency` printed `p95 1341 ms` for forty calls. What does that say?
hint: The percentile takes a position in the sorted list.

choices.text: The average of the forty calls, added up and divided, was 1341 ms
choices.why: That would be a mean; `pl latency` prints none.

choices.text: 95 of the forty calls took 1341 ms
choices.why: There were only forty calls; 95 is a percentage.

choices.text: Only two calls of the forty were slower than 1341 ms
choices.why: Right: the 38th of forty in order.

choices.text: The slowest of all the forty calls in the run took 1341 ms
choices.why: The slowest is `max`, 1371 ms.

prompt: `pl cost` reports 5.1072 cents for forty calls of `v3-examples`. How much is one call, in cents?
At the lab's prices (300 cents a million input tokens, 1500 a million output tokens), what do 1000 calls cost if each reads 200 tokens and writes 40, in cents?
hint: Per call: 200 × 300 + 40 × 1500 millionths of a cent.

prompt: Why does the harness multiply integers and round only once, at the end?

choices.text: Integers are faster to multiply than floats
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

choices.text: A float cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly, so sums of them drift, and a bill must not
choices.why: Right. Whole tokens times whole prices is exact; one stated rounding at the end.

choices.text: Python has no floating-point numbers
choices.why: It does: `0.1 + 0.2` is one.

choices.text: Providers forbid fractions of a cent
choices.why: Per-token prices are fractions of a cent; that is why the unit is millionths.

prompt: Output was under 14% of the tokens of the `v3-examples` run. Why was it 44% of the cost?

choices.text: Output tokens are longer words than input tokens, so the stand-in counts each of them twice
choices.why: A token is a token; the count is not doubled.

choices.text: The harness rounds output costs up and input costs down
choices.why: It rounds once, at the end, on the total.

choices.text: Each costs five times as much
choices.why: Right: 1500 cents a million against 300.

choices.text: The cache was writing them on every call
choices.why: The cache was off: `cache_write` is 0.

prompt: Tokens are whole and prices are whole cents per million, so tokens times price is an exact count of ___ of a cent.
hint: One cent divided a million ways.

prompt: `--set max_tokens=30` on `v3-examples` cut the p95 from 1341 ms to 1138. What happened to the score, and why?

choices.text: Unchanged, because the model wrote shorter answers to fit
choices.why: A cap does not make the model write less; it stops it.

choices.text: It fell to 1 of 40: replies were cut mid-string and stopped being JSON
choices.why: Right. `stop: max_tokens` says the cap, not the model, ended the reply.

choices.text: It rose, because shorter is better
choices.why: It fell from 36 to 1.

choices.text: It fell a little, and only on the long messages whose summaries ran past the cap
choices.why: It fell on 35 of the 36 that had passed.

prompt: The longest good answer to `v3-examples` was 46 tokens. Where should its output cap sit?
hint: A cap is a ceiling, not a target.

choices.text: At 30, to force every answer to be shorter and cheaper
choices.why: That cut every reply mid-string.

choices.text: At exactly 46, to the token
choices.why: Leaves no room for a good answer a little longer than any seen.

choices.text: Above 46, to stop only runaway replies
choices.why: Right: it saves money only on replies that were going wrong.

choices.text: Nowhere: caps never save anything at all
choices.why: They save on runaway replies.

prompt: Which of these are ways the lesson gives to make calls cheaper? Choose all that apply.
hint: Fewer tokens, cheaper tokens, or waiting.

choices.text: Fewer examples in the prompt
choices.why: Yes: fewer input tokens on every call.

choices.text: Asking for a shorter summary
choices.why: Yes: fewer output tokens, the dearer kind.

choices.text: Sending work that can wait through a batch interface
choices.why: Yes, where a provider sells one.

choices.text: Rounding each call's cost down to the cent
choices.why: That changes the report, not the bill, and breaks the arithmetic.

prompt: Why does the lesson give no numbers for routing easy messages to a cheaper model?
hint: What would there be to route between?

choices.text: The lab's stand-in is a single model with one price, so any number would be invented
choices.why: Right. The method carries over: route, then compare on the same test sets.

choices.text: Routing never saves money
choices.why: It does where a cheaper model is good enough for some messages.

choices.text: Providers forbid it
choices.why: Nothing forbids sending different messages to different models.

choices.text: Routing cannot be tested
choices.why: It is tested like any version: run the pipeline over the test sets.

prompt: Which work suits a provider's batch interface?

choices.text: Sorting a customer's message while they wait on the support page
choices.why: Somebody is waiting; a batch returns results later.

choices.text: Re-sorting last year's archive
choices.why: Right: nobody is watching, so later is fine.

choices.text: A chat reply that the customer expects within a few seconds
choices.why: A batch can take hours.

choices.text: Any call that has failed once and needs to be retried quickly
choices.why: Quickly is exactly what a batch does not promise.

prompt: Removing the examples gave `fixed 1, broken 3` and a sign test of 0.625. What does that p value tell you?

choices.text: Forty messages are too few to tell the two prompts apart by count; it does not say they are equal
choices.why: Right: even four out of four would only have reached 0.125.

choices.text: The prompts are equally good
choices.why: No evidence of a difference is not evidence of no difference.

choices.text: The cheaper prompt is better
choices.why: It passed fewer.

choices.text: The run should be repeated until p falls below 0.05
choices.why: At temperature 0 the stand-in gives the same answers every time.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer the p95 to the mean when judging latency?

choices.text: The mean is harder to compute when the calls arrive from many different machines
choices.why: It is easier, and that is not the reason.

choices.text: The p95 is always the larger number, so it is the safer one to quote in any report
choices.why: The point is what the reader experiences, not which number is larger.

choices.text: A person waiting feels the slow calls, and the mean blends them away
choices.why: Right: the mean can fall while the slow calls get slower.

choices.text: The stand-in has no mean
choices.why: `pl latency` simply does not print one.

prompt: From the two `pl cost` lines, how many cents a million calls did removing the examples save (127,680 against 85,043)?
Three of the cheaper prompt's replies were not JSON. Why does the lesson weigh that more than a wrong urgency?
hint: What does the routing program do with each?

choices.text: Because a JSON failure costs the provider more tokens to produce than an ordinary wrong label
choices.why: The cost is in what happens next, not in the tokens.

choices.text: Because the sign test counts them twice
choices.why: Each message counts once.

choices.text: Because they are slower to generate than the JSON replies
choices.why: Speed is not the problem with them.

choices.text: It routes nothing
choices.why: Right: a wrong urgency still routes the message; an unreadable reply needs a retry or a person.

prompt: Put the lesson's order for cutting cost in sequence, first step first.
items: Trade answers for money, with the broken messages named

prompt: Match each change to what the lab showed it did.

pairs.right: A third cheaper, three replies not JSON

pairs.left: Three times the input, slightly less output
pairs.right: A median 44 ms higher and a lower p95

pairs.left: Integers instead of floats for money

right_distractors: A cache hit on every call

prompt: A colleague halves the summary's length and reports the mean latency fell by 8%. What would you ask for before accepting it?
hint: A saving is a change; latency is felt in the tail.

choices.text: Nothing: shorter output is always better
choices.why: It may break answers, and the mean may hide the tail.

choices.text: The comparison on every test set, with the broken messages, and the p95
choices.why: Right: score unchanged, tokens down, and the slow calls not slower.

choices.text: A rerun at a higher temperature, to see whether the latency still falls by the same amount
choices.why: Temperature is a separate change and tells you nothing about this one.

choices.text: The provider's price list
choices.why: The prices did not change; the question is what the change did.
